{{Short description|Equation whose side(s) describe a transcendental function}}
{{more citations needed|date = October 2011}}
[[File:Herschel - Description of a machine for resolving by inspection certain important forms of transcendental equations, 1832 - 687143.tiff|thumb|[[John Herschel]], ''Description of a machine for resolving by inspection certain important forms of transcendental equations'', 1832]]

In [[applied mathematics]], a '''transcendental equation''' is an [[equation]] over the [[real number|real]] (or [[complex number|complex]]) numbers that is not [[algebraic equation|algebraic]], that is, if at least one of its sides describes a [[transcendental function]].<ref>{{cite book | author=I.N. Bronstein and K.A. Semendjajew and G. Musiol and H. Mühlig | title=Taschenbuch der Mathematik | location=Frankfurt/Main |
publisher=Harri Deutsch | year=2005 |language=German}} Here: Sect.1.6.4.1, p.45. The domain of equations is left implicit throughout the book.</ref>
Examples include:

:<math>\begin{align}
  x &= e^{-x} \\
  x &= \cos x \\
  2^x &= x^2
\end{align}</math>

A transcendental equation may involve also [[Elementary function#Non-elementary functions|non-elementary functions]], although most published examples do not.

In some cases, a transcendental equation can be solved by transforming it into an equivalent algebraic equation.
Some such transformations are sketched [[#Transformation into an algebraic equation|below]]; [[computer algebra]] systems may provide more elaborated transformations.{{efn|For example, according to the [[Wolfram Mathematica]] tutorial page on [https://reference.wolfram.com/language/tutorial/ManipulatingEquationsAndInequalities.html#16840 equation solving], both <math>2^x = x</math> and <math>e^x + x + 1 = 0</math> can be solved by symbolic expressions, while <math>x = \cos x</math> can only be solved approximatively.}}

In general, however, only approximate solutions can be found.<ref>Bronstein et al., p.45-46</ref>

==Transformation into an algebraic equation==
Ad hoc methods exist for some classes of transcendental equations in one variable to transform them into algebraic equations which then might be solved.

===Exponential equations===
If the unknown, say ''x'', occurs only in exponents:
* applying the [[natural logarithm]] to both sides may yield an algebraic equation,<ref>Bronstein et al., Sect.1.6.4.2.a, p.46</ref> e.g.
: <math>4^x = 3^{x^2-1} \cdot 2^{5x}</math> transforms to <math>x \ln 4 = (x^2-1) \ln 3 + 5x \ln 2</math>, which simplifies to <math>x^2 \ln 3 + x(5 \ln 2 - \ln 4) -\ln 3 = 0</math>, which has the solutions <math>x = \frac{ -3 \ln 2 \pm \sqrt{9(\ln 2)^2 - 4 (\ln 3)^2} }{ 2 \ln 3 } .</math>
: This will not work if addition occurs "at the base line", as in <math>4^x = 3^{x^2-1} + 2^{5x} .</math>
* if all "base constants" can be written as integer or rational powers of some number ''q'', then substituting ''y''=''q''<sup>''x''</sup> may succeed, e.g.
: <math>2^{x-1} + 4^{x-2} - 8^{x-2} = 0</math> transforms, using ''y''=2<sup>''x''</sup>, to  <math>\frac{1}{2} y + \frac{1}{16} y^2 - \frac{1}{64} y^3 = 0</math> which has the solutions <math>y \in \{ 0, -4, 8\}</math>, hence <math>x= \log_2 8 = 3</math> is the only real solution.<ref>Bronstein et al., Sect.1.6.4.2.b, p.46</ref>
: This will not work if a square or a higher power of ''x'' occurs in an exponent, or if the "base constants" do not "share" a common ''q''.
* sometimes, substituting ''y''=''x''e<sup>''x''</sup> may obtain an algebraic equation; after the solutions for ''y'' are known, those for ''x'' can be obtained by applying the [[Lambert W function]],{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} e.g.:
: <math>x^2e^{2x} + 2 = 3x e^x</math> transforms to <math>y^2 + 2 = 3y,</math> which has the solutions <math>y \in \{1,2\},</math> hence <math>x \in \{ W_0(1), W_0(2), W_{-1}(1), W_{-1}(2) \}</math>, where <math>W_0</math> and <math>W_{-1}</math> denote the real-valued branches of the multivalued <math>W</math> function.

===Logarithmic equations===
If the unknown ''x'' occurs only in arguments of a [[logarithm]] function:
* applying [[exponentiation]] to both sides may yield an algebraic equation, e.g.
:<math>2 \log_5 (3x-1) - \log_5 (12x+1) = 0</math> transforms, using exponentiation to base <math>5</math>, to <math>\frac{ (3x-1)^2 }{ 12x+1 } = 1,</math> which has the solutions <math>x \in \{ 0, 2\} .</math> If only real numbers are considered, <math>x = 0</math> is not a solution, as it leads to a non-real [[subterm|subexpression]] <math>\log_5(-1)</math> in the given equation.
:This requires the original equation to consist of [[integer]]-coefficient linear combinations of logarithms w.r.t. a unique base, and the logarithm arguments to be polynomials in ''x''.<ref>Bronstein et al., Sect.1.6.4.3.b, p.46</ref>
* if all "logarithm calls" have a unique base <math>b</math> and a unique argument expression <math>f(x),</math> then substituting <math>y = \log_b (f(x))</math> may lead to a simpler equation,<ref>Bronstein et al., Sect.1.6.4.3.a, p.46</ref> e.g.
: <math>5 \ln(\sin x^2) + 6 = 7 \sqrt{ \ln(\sin x^2) + 8 }</math> transforms, using <math>y = \ln(\sin x^2) ,</math> to <math>5 y + 6 = 7 \sqrt{ y + 8 },</math> which is [[algebraic equation|algebraic]] and has the single solution <math>y=\frac{89}{25}</math>.{{efn|Squaring both sides obtains <math>25y^2+60y+36 = 49 \cdot (y+8)</math> which has the additional solution <math>y=-4</math>; however, the latter does not solve the unsquared equation.}} After that, applying inverse operations to the substitution equation yields <math>x = \sqrt{ \arcsin \exp y } = \sqrt{ \arcsin \exp \frac{89}{25} }.</math>

===Trigonometric equations===
If the unknown ''x'' occurs only as argument of [[trigonometric function]]s:
* applying [[List of trigonometric identities#Pythagorean identities|Pythagorean identities]] and trigonometric [[Trigonometric functions#Sum and difference formulas|sum]] and [[List of trigonometric identities#Multiple-angle and half-angle formulae|multiple]] formulas, arguments of the forms <math>\sin(nx+a), \cos(mx+b), \tan(lx+c), ...</math> with integer <math>n,m,l,...</math> might all be transformed to arguments of the form, say, <math>\sin x</math>. After that, substituting <math>y = \sin(x)</math> yields an algebraic equation,<ref>Bronstein et al., Sect.1.6.4.4, p.46-47</ref> e.g.
: <math>\sin(x+a) = (\cos^2 x) - 1</math> transforms to <math>(\sin x)(\cos a) + \sqrt{ 1 - \sin^2 x }(\sin a) = 1 - (\sin^2 x) - 1</math>, and, after substitution, to <math>y (\cos a) + \sqrt{ 1 - y^2 }(\sin a) = - y^2</math> which is algebraic{{efn|over an appropriate field, containing <math>\sin a</math> and <math>\cos a</math>}} and can be solved. After that, applying <math>x = 2k\pi + \arcsin y</math> obtains the solutions.

===Hyperbolic equations===
If the unknown ''x'' occurs only in linear expressions inside arguments of [[hyperbolic function]]s,
* unfolding them by their defining exponential expressions and substituting <math>y = \exp(x)</math> yields an algebraic equation,<ref>Bronstein et al., Sect.1.6.4.5, p.47</ref> e.g.
: <math>3 \cosh x = 4 + \sinh (2x-6)</math> unfolds to <math>\frac{3}{2} (e^x + \frac{1}{e^x}) = 4 + \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{(e^x)^2}{e^6} - \frac{e^6}{(e^x)^2} \right) ,</math> which transforms to the  equation <math>\frac{3}{2} (y + \frac{1}{y}) = 4 + \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{y^2}{e^6} - \frac{e^6}{y^2} \right) ,</math> which is algebraic{{efn|over an appropriate field, containing <math>e^6</math>}} and can be solved. Applying <math>x = \ln y</math> obtains the solutions of the original equation.

==Approximate solutions==
[[File:Sin x = ln x svg.svg|thumb|250px|Graphical solution of sin(''x'')=ln(''x'')]]
Approximate numerical solutions to transcendental equations can be found using [[numerical solution|numerical]], analytical approximations, or graphical methods.

These equations can be solved by direct iteration by reordering the equation into the form <math>x=f(x)</math> and
making an initial guess <math>x_0</math>, computing <math>f(x)</math> which becomes <math>x_1</math> and substituting it back into <math>f(x)</math>, etc. Convergence may be very slow. Some reorderings may diverge, so some other reordering that converges must be found. <math>f(x)</math> must be continuous and "sufficiently smooth" or the method may fail. 

Numerical methods for solving arbitrary equations are called [[root-finding algorithms]]. By rearranging the equation into the form <math>f(x)=0</math>, if <math>f(x)</math> is continuous and differentiable, [[Newton's method]] involving taking the derivative of <math>f(x)</math>, is a common iterative method of approximating a root; an initial guess <math>x_0</math> must be "sufficiently close" to the root of interest to converge to it. 

In some cases, the equation can be well approximated using  [[Taylor series]] near the zero. For example, for <math>k \approx 1</math>, the solutions of <math>\sin x = k x</math> are approximately those of <math>(1-k) x - x^3/6=0</math>, namely <math>x=0</math> and <math>x = \plusmn \sqrt{6} \sqrt{1-k}</math>.

For a graphical solution, one method is to set each side of a single-variable transcendental equation equal to a [[dependent variable]] and plot the two [[Graph of a function|graphs]], using their intersecting points to find solutions (see picture).

== Other solutions ==
* Some transcendental systems of high-order equations can be solved by “separation” of the unknowns, reducing them to algebraic equations.<ref>[http://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=zvmmf&paperid=7414&option_lang=eng V. A. Varyuhin, S. A. Kas'yanyuk, “On a certain method for solving nonlinear systems of a special type”], Zh. Vychisl. Mat. Mat. Fiz., 6:2 (1966),  347–352; U.S.S.R. Comput. Math. Math. Phys., 6:2 (1966), 214–221</ref><ref name="book">V.A. Varyukhin, Fundamental Theory of Multichannel Analysis (VA PVO SV, Kyiv, 1993) [in Russian]</ref>
* The following can also be used when solving transcendental equations/inequalities: If <math>x_0</math> is a solution to the equation <math>f(x)=g(x)</math> and <math>f(x)\leq c\leq g(x)</math>, then this solution must satisfy <math>f(x_0)=g(x_0)=c</math>. For example, we want to solve <math>\log_{2}\left(3+2x-x^{2}\right)=\tan^{2}\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)+\cot^{2}\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)</math>. The given equation is defined for <math>-1<x<3</math>. Let <math>f(x)=\log_{2}\left(3+2x-x^{2}\right)</math> and <math>g(x)=\tan^{2}\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)+\cot^{2}\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)</math>. It is easy to show that <math>f(x)\leq 2</math> and <math>g(x)\geq 2</math> so if there is a solution to the equation, it must satisfy <math>f(x)=g(x)=2</math>. From <math>f(x)=2</math> we get <math>x=1\in(-1,3)</math>. Indeed, <math>f(1)=g(1)=2</math> and so <math>x=1</math> is the only real solution to the equation.
